fit_paragraphs.text: Prof. Carpuat's CLIP Lab sits at the intersection of my three research directions. Her work on cross-lingual alignment in multilingual LLMs maps directly onto the degradation I measured in code-switched Tamil–English inputs [lib:cv], and her SpeechQE line on direct speech translation connects to my wav2vec2-style Tamil ASR project [lib:cv][lib:interests]. I am also drawn to [paper:W4401042399], which uses error annotations to guide LLM post-editing — a framing I want to extend to low-resource Dravidian languages where MT errors cluster differently than in high-resource pairs. The lab's human-centered work on AI for non-native speakers [paper:W4409736318] frames evaluation exactly as I believe it should be: around real communicative needs rather than translated benchmarks [lib:interests][advisor:Marine Carpuat].

Prof. Rudinger's research on evaluation methodology and cultural fairness in LLMs aligns with the second axis of my PhD plan: building assessments that measure what multilingual users actually need rather than proxy English-centric metrics [lib:interests][advisor:Rachel Rudinger]. Her work diagnosing flaws in multiple-choice LLM evaluation [paper:W4412886673] is directly relevant to my finding that standard benchmarks miss code-switching failures entirely [lib:cv]. The discrimination-in-hiring study [paper:W4402671226] shows her group treats social harm as a first-class measurement target — a lens I want to apply to health and government information access in Tamil and Kannada [lib:interests]. A co-supervision arrangement with Prof. Carpuat, whose lab already collaborates with Prof. Rudinger [paper:W4402640336], would cover both adaptation and evaluation rigorously.

Prof. Wiegreffe's mechanistic interpretability work offers tools I want to apply to a concrete question: why do open LLMs fail disproportionately on code-switched inputs [lib:cv][lib:interests]? Understanding the internal representations behind those 18–26 point drops requires exactly the circuit-level analysis her group pursues [advisor:Sarah Wiegreffe]. Her paper interrogating what 'mechanistic' actually means [paper:W4404784049] is a useful corrective for the field, and her finding that easy training data can transfer to hard tasks [paper:W4402671639] suggests low-resource language adaptation may benefit from interpretability-guided data selection — a direction I have not yet seen explored for Dravidian languages [lib:interests]. While her primary focus is not multilingual NLP, the methodological fit is strong enough that I would want to discuss shared supervision.

sop.text:
In 2025 I built a Tamil–English code-switched evaluation set of 2,400 sentences and tested two open 7B models on it [lib:cv]. Both lost between 18 and 26 points relative to their monolingual Tamil baselines [lib:cv]. People in Chennai do not speak monolingual Tamil to a chatbot; they switch registers mid-sentence. That measurement became my first-author workshop paper at an ACL-family Student Research Workshop [lib:cv] and convinced me that evaluation is where multilingual NLP is most broken: we benchmark on translated English data and declare success for populations who never interact that way [lib:interests].

The following summer I worked at Microsoft Research India under Dr. Anjali Mehra [lib:cv]. The project was tokenizer adaptation for Kannada: adding 6,000 domain-relevant tokens to a SentencePiece vocabulary cut the average token count per sentence by 41% and improved downstream QA F1 by 3.4 points at the same fine-tuning budget [lib:cv]. The practical lesson was that targeted, cheap structural changes to a model's input representation can matter as much as expensive continued pretraining — a result I want to generalize to other Dravidian languages [lib:interests].

In a parallel course project I trained a wav2vec2-style model on 40 hours of Tamil radio audio and reached 31% WER on a held-out set [lib:cv]. Most Tamil data is spoken rather than written, so speech-text pipelines are not optional infrastructure; they are the primary access point for a large fraction of potential users [lib:interests]. That project also exposed the limits of small supervised sets, which drives my interest in self-supervised and parameter-efficient methods [lib:interests].

For a PhD I want to pursue three connected problems. First: parameter-efficient and data-efficient adaptation of LLMs to low-resource Indian languages, combining tokenizer redesign with PEFT methods such as LoRA [lib:interests]. Second: evaluation frameworks that measure code-switching robustness, cultural grounding, and faithfulness rather than translated-benchmark accuracy [lib:interests]. Third: speech-text models that can be trained on tens, not thousands, of hours of audio [lib:interests].

At UMD I am particularly drawn to Prof. Marine Carpuat's CLIP Lab. Her group's work on cross-lingual alignment in multilingual LLMs addresses the same generalization gap I measured empirically, and her error-annotation-guided post-editing work [paper:W4401042399] frames LLM output quality as something to be diagnosed and repaired — a framing I want to extend to low-resource Dravidian settings. Her lab's research on AI for non-native speakers [paper:W4409736318] grounds evaluation in real communicative needs rather than aggregate scores, which matches exactly how I think about the Tamil–English code-switching problem. I also want to engage with Prof. Rachel Rudinger's work on evaluation methodology; her critique of multiple-choice LLM evaluation [paper:W4412886673] makes explicit the measurement failures I keep running into empirically, and her collaboration with Prof. Carpuat [paper:W4402640336] suggests a natural joint research space around semantics and fairness in multilingual contexts [advisor:Rachel Rudinger].

My CGPA is 9.21/10, placing me in the top 5% of my department [lib:profile]. I hold the Institute Merit Scholarship for three consecutive years [lib:cv] and finished second at the Inter-NIT hackathon 2025 with a multilingual FAQ bot for a district hospital [lib:cv]. As a teaching assistant for a 120-student machine learning course and organizer of an NLP reading group of roughly 25 members, I have learned that explaining a method to someone who does not yet see why it matters is its own form of research training [lib:cv].

I expect to complete my B.Tech in May 2027 and am applying for Fall 2027 entry [lib:profile]. The problems I care about — making large models work for speakers of Tamil, Kannada, and Hindi with limited data and realistic speech input — require sustained, collaborative research, and the combination of multilingual NLP depth and evaluation rigor at UMD CS is where I want to do that work.

emails.subject: Prospective PhD student (Fall 2027) — multilingual LLM adaptation and evaluation for Indian languages
emails.body:
Dear Prof. Carpuat,

I am a final-year B.Tech student at NIT Tiruchirappalli applying to the UMD CS PhD program for Fall 2027. My research focuses on efficient adaptation of LLMs to low-resource Indian languages and on evaluation methods that capture code-switching and cultural grounding rather than translated-benchmark accuracy.

I read your recent paper "Guiding Large Language Models to Post-Edit Machine Translation with Error Annotations" (NAACL 2024) with close attention. The idea of using structured error annotations to guide LLM corrections is one I want to extend to Tamil and Kannada, where MT errors have different distributions than in the high-resource pairs your paper addresses. I also built a Tamil–English code-switched evaluation set showing 18–26 point drops for open 7B models, which became a workshop paper at an ACL-family venue this year.

Could you tell me whether you are planning to take PhD students for the Fall 2027 cycle? I would be glad to share my CV and to discuss how my work might fit your lab's current directions.

Thank you for your time.

Priya Raman

emails.subject: Prospective PhD student (Fall 2027) — LLM evaluation methodology for multilingual settings
emails.body:
Dear Prof. Rudinger,

I am a final-year B.Tech student at NIT Tiruchirappalli applying to the UMD CS PhD program for Fall 2027. I saw on your website that you are planning to admit PhD students for this cycle and wanted to reach out directly.

Your 2025 ACL paper "Which of These Best Describes Multiple Choice Evaluation with LLMs?" articulates a failure mode I keep running into empirically: when I tested open 7B models on a Tamil–English code-switched set I built, the performance drop was invisible to standard translated benchmarks. I am interested in developing evaluation frameworks — drawing on the methodological critique your group advances — that are sensitive to code-switching, cultural grounding, and the specific ways low-resource languages fail. I also see natural connections to your collaborative work with Prof. Carpuat.

I would welcome the chance to discuss my background further. I am happy to share my CV and a draft of my workshop paper if that would be useful.

Thank you for your time.

Priya Raman

emails.subject: Prospective PhD student (Fall 2027) — mechanistic interpretability applied to multilingual model failures
emails.body:
Dear Prof. Wiegreffe,

I am a final-year B.Tech student at NIT Tiruchirappalli applying to the UMD CS PhD program for Fall 2027. My research is on multilingual LLM adaptation and evaluation for low-resource Indian languages, and I am writing because your work on mechanistic interpretability addresses a question I have not been able to answer empirically.

In my workshop paper I showed that open 7B models lose 18–26 accuracy points on Tamil–English code-switched inputs compared with monolingual Tamil. I know the number but not the mechanism. Your 2024 BlackBoxNLP paper "Mechanistic?" raises exactly the conceptual questions I would need to answer before designing a principled fix. I am also curious whether the finding in "The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Easy Training Data for Hard Tasks" generalizes to cross-lingual transfer, where the notion of "easy" data is less obvious.

Are you planning to take PhD students for Fall 2027? I am happy to share my CV.

Thank you.

Priya Raman
